source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: 100 psychology studies replicated with high power. Replication effects were half the size of originals. Replication success was better predicted by strength of original evidence than by team traits.
numbers: 97% of originals significant; 36% of replications significant; 47% of original effect sizes inside the replication 95% CI; 39% subjectively rated as replicated; 68% significant when original and replication pooled (assuming no bias). Abstract text read via Europe PMC (full paper blocked, 403).
limits: Abstract only. Corrects K02: 36% is the significance rate, 39% is the subjective rating (Serra-Garcia used 39%).
agent_relevance: Discount a first-pass effect by about half and rely on evidence strength, not on who ran it: a held-out recheck should compare against the original CI, not only a p-value.

source: Gilbert, King, Pettigrew and Wilson (2016) Comment on 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science'
finding: Critique: OSC contains three statistical errors and its data are consistent with high reproducibility.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures were read.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC. The specific error types and numbers were not read and are not recorded here.
agent_relevance: A failed recheck can itself be a noisy or non-equivalent test. A held-out check should use the same protocol as the first run, else a mismatch looks like a failure.

source: Anderson et al. (2016) Response to Comment on 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science'
finding: OSC reply: Gilbert et al. are limited by statistical misconceptions and selective reading of correlational data. Both optimistic and pessimistic conclusions are possible; neither is yet warranted.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures.
limits: Authors' own reply, so not independent. The dispute stayed unresolved.
agent_relevance: Replication verdicts depend on the criterion. Report several indicators (significance, CI coverage, effect ratio) for an agent's own rechecks.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015
finding: 21 experiments from Nature and Science replicated with preregistered analysis plans reviewed by the original authors and samples about 5 times larger.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) significant in same direction; mean replication effect about 50% of original; alternative indicators 12 (57%) to 14 (67%); Bayesian true-positive rate 67%; true positives' relative effect size 71%; peer beliefs strongly related to replicability.
limits: Abstract read from the Nature page. Corrects K02 and b21: the 75% figure was second-hand; primary says about 50% (71% for estimated true positives).
agent_relevance: Even top-journal, preregistered, high-power rechecks lose half the effect. Both false positives and inflated true effects cause shrinkage.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: 28 findings replicated across 125 samples; replicability depended more on the effect than on the sample or setting.
numbers: 15,305 participants, 36 countries; 15 of 28 (54%) significant same direction at p<.05; 14 (50%) at p<.0001; 21 (75%) smaller than original; median d original 0.60 vs replication 0.15; 9 (32%) opposite direction; 11 (39%) significant heterogeneity; lab vs online and WEIRD vs non-WEIRD explained little.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC (preprint record). Corrects b23: 15 of 28 at p<.05, not 14 (14 under the strict criterion).
agent_relevance: A failed recheck is rarely explained away by site or sample, so it should lower confidence rather than be dismissed as a moderator.

source: Dreber et al. (2025) Examining the replicability of online experiments selected by a decision market
finding: Social scientists trading on replication outcomes picked studies that did replicate more often: markets carry real signal.
numbers: 162 traders, 41 MTurk experiments from PNAS 2015-18; 12 highest-priced replicated 83%, 12 lowest 33%; overall 54% replicated (26 studies replicated); replicated effects averaged 45% of original; 54-62% across indicators.
limits: Human forecasters, not LLMs. Only 26 replicated studies; 12 per group.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: shows the target an LLM ensemble must hit (83% vs 33% split). No LLM-ensemble replication forecast study was found in this search.

source: Panickssery, Bowman and Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: LLM judges can tell their own text from others and prefer it. Self-preference grows with self-recognition, shown by fine-tuning.
numbers: GPT-4 73.5% accurate at picking its own summary among itself, two LLMs and humans; GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 over 90% self-recognition after 500 fine-tuning examples; pairwise order flips 25% (GPT-4), 58% (GPT-3.5), 89% (Llama 2); example-level Kendall tau 0.41 for GPT-3.5 on XSUM before tuning, up to 0.65 in one tuned setting; XSUM and CNN/DM summaries.
limits: Summarisation only, not peer review. Causality inferred from fine-tuning; Table 1 columns not fully mapped.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a reviewer that shares a model with the author will likely over-approve; use a different model family or held-out execution for G3.

source: Wataoka, Takahashi and Ri (2025) Self-preference bias in LLM-as-a-judge
finding: GPT-4 shows the largest self-preference among 8 judges on Chatbot Arena pairs; bias tracks low perplexity of the text, not authorship alone.
numbers: GPT-4 recall on human-favoured responses 0.945 vs 0.425 on human-disfavoured, gap 0.520; demographic-parity self-preference score GPT-4 0.749, Vicuna-13b 0.382, GPT-3.5 0.191, others near 0; all judges rate low-perplexity text higher than humans do.
limits: Chatbot Arena dialogue, not scientific review. Perplexity unavailable for GPT-4, so the mechanism rests on open models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: agreement between same-family author and judge is partly familiarity of style. Ranking by held-out outcome avoids it.

source: Laurito et al. (2025) AI-AI bias: large language models favor communications generated by large language models
finding: LLMs choosing between human-written and LLM-written descriptions prefer the LLM-written ones, more than human evaluators do; the effect is smaller for paper abstracts than for products.
numbers: Products 109 items (220 trials per model), 186 paper-abstract trials, plus movie plots; GPT-3.5, GPT-4-1106, Llama-3.1-70B, Mixtral-8x22B, Qwen2.5-72B; first-item bias 46.6-73.2% (products), 40.2-58.1% (abstracts); order swapped to control.
limits: Abstracts were LLM-written from the full paper text; headline preference sizes for abstracts not extracted. Not a reviewer-score study.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: an LLM reviewer of LLM-written work is advantaged. Keep authoring and checking models distinct; swap orders.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Self-correction helps only when an oracle tells the model whether its answer is right. Without that signal accuracy drops.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 74.7 after 2 rounds, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 41.8, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0; with oracle labels GSM8K 95.5 (GPT-4 97.5), HotpotQA 49-59; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0, CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 80.0; GPT-3.5 keeps first answer 74.7% on GSM8K and changes right to wrong more often than wrong to right.
limits: 2023 models, three benchmarks, prompts from earlier papers. Reasoning models later may differ.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: self-critique without external signal is not a recheck. A held-out check supplies the missing outside signal; test it against self-critique at equal calls.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (debate versus self-consistency)
finding: At equal response counts, simple majority voting (self-consistency) matches or beats multi-agent debate.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 1 response 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2; debate 83.2 at 6 and 83.0 at 9 responses per the table; the paper says debate only slightly beats voting at 3 and underperforms it at equal larger counts.
limits: Extracted table is interleaved; only the self-consistency row values are certain. Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: any claim that a checking scaffold beats extra samples must be compared at equal calls. Voting is the baseline to beat.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Whether verifiers and revisions beat plain sampling depends on prompt difficulty. Allocating test-time compute per prompt beats best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy matches best-of-N using about 4x less test-time compute (revisions and PRM search, MATH, PaLM 2-S*); in a FLOPs-matched comparison a smaller model with test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model where it has non-trivial success.
limits: Needed capability-specific fine-tuning for revision and verification; one model family; math only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: at equal tokens, verifying or revising pays on easier items and sampling on harder ones; route recheck effort by difficulty.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Where an automatic verifier exists, more samples plus the verifier turn coverage into accuracy. Without one, majority voting and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct 15.9% (1 sample) -> 56% (250 samples) vs single-sample state of the art 43%; GSM8K/MATH subsets coverage 98.44% at 10,000 samples while voting and reward-model selection plateau near 100 samples.
limits: The verifier is unit tests or proof checkers; the gain comes from an external check, not from the model judging itself.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: strongest support that an external held-out check outperforms spending the same tokens on self-selection.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: flaky and imperfect verifiers
finding: Verifiers are themselves imperfect: tests can be flaky or reject correct solutions.
numbers: 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems have flaky test suites that sometimes fail even the gold patch; CodeContests has false-negative correct solutions; results similar after removing flaky items.
limits: Descriptive; effect on final accuracy small.
agent_relevance: A held-out check must be rerun and itself checked or it adds noise.

source: Haldar and Hockenmaier (2025) Rating roulette: self-inconsistency in LLM-as-a-judge frameworks
finding: Same judge, same prompt, repeated runs: agreement with itself is low, task dependent, and not fixed by more runs.
numbers: SummaC binary labels, Krippendorff alpha over 3 runs: Llama 3.1 0.326, DeepSeek-R1 0.628, Qwen3 0.788 (threshold 0.8); 5 runs gave no meaningful change; SummEval: high on coherence and consistency, very low on fluency.
limits: Summarisation judging, 3 open models, temperature 0.6; no human self-reliability measured, so no direct comparison with the 23-26% committee figure.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: one LLM judgment is a noisy draw; use repeated runs as a flag and treat unstable items as unresolved.

source: Haldar and Hockenmaier (2025) Rating roulette: MT-Bench result
finding: On pairwise multi-turn chat judging, self-reliability is much lower.
numbers: MT-Bench alpha: Llama 3.1 0.265, DeepSeek-R1 0.507, Qwen3 0.563; Qwen3 gave the same judgment on all 3 runs for only 61.3% of items.
limits: Different metric from committee disagreement; do not equate the roughly 39% non-identical items with 23-26%.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: LLM judges are self-inconsistent on open tasks at a rate at least comparable to human committees, so single-run verdicts need aggregation.

source: Performance of AI tools in citing retracted literature: content analysis (2026)
finding: Nine free GenAI tools could not reliably detect, exclude or flag retracted papers.
numbers: 15 retracted articles (10 most cited, 5 most recent), 5 questions each, repeated twice; best tool ChatGPT 5 fully correct on 8 of 15 (53.3%); research-focused tools SciSpace, ScienceOS, Consensus had no fully correct set; error rates over 40% in several tools for topic overviews including retracted work without warning.
limits: Small sample (15 papers), free-tier tools in 2025. Tests no refutation-tag fix.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly: persistence of refuted claims is current. No study tested a refutation tag in memory; this stays open and is cheap to test ourselves.

source: Many AI analysts, one dataset: navigating the agentic data science multiverse (PNAS 2026)
finding: Autonomous LLM analysts on the same data and hypothesis produce human-like dispersion in effect sizes, p-values and conclusions.
numbers: 4,946 runs, 3 datasets, 4 base LLMs, 5 personas; 3,303 (67%) passed an AI auditor; about 30 compliant runs per cell; human benchmarks cited: Silberzahn 29 teams (20 significant, 9 not), Breznau 73 teams.
limits: Auditor is an LLM; few datasets; no preregistration arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: analytic flexibility is large for LLM agents too, so committing the analysis before running is the lever Ioannidis corollary 3 names.

source: Many AI analysts, one dataset: persona steering and auditing
finding: Telling the analyst to confirm raises support rates; an auditor screening the transcript removes the most aggressive runs but not all steering.
numbers: Negative-to-Strong-confirmation-seeking gap in support rate 34 points (anes-views) to 66 points (metr-rct); negative vs positive personas differ modestly; auditor filtering narrows but does not eliminate the gap; confirmation personas search specifications and overclaim.
limits: Persona instructions explicitly invite p-hacking, an upper bound of natural behavior.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 8: confirmation-framed prompts shift conclusions; an independent audit of the full transcript is a partial remedy. Commit the spec first and audit deviations.

source: Begley and Ellis (2012) Drug development: raise standards for preclinical cancer research
finding: Industry team could not confirm most landmark preclinical findings (from memory).
numbers: Not opened: only the title was retrieved via Europe PMC (no abstract). The remembered 6 of 53 (11%) is unverified.
limits: Paywalled; methods unpublished; Prinz 2011 gave 20-25%. Do not cite the number.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only partly closed: Begley and Ellis figures stay unverified.
